title: Mountain Ranges Around the World
summary: A tour of the world's great mountain ranges, where they sit, how they formed, and how they shape the climate, borders, and wildlife around them.
poll: Mountains make a country a better place to live.

versions.title: Mountains of the World
versions.text:
Look at a map. Do you see long lines of tall hills? Those are mountains. A long line of hills is a range. Ranges sit all over the world.

One big range sits far away. It runs down one side of the land. It sits near the sea. Some of its peaks are old and round. Animals graze there.

A range sits far north. Rivers start high on its slopes. Some flow one way. Some flow the other way.

One range sits in a cold land. People ski on its snowy slopes. It makes a border between two lands.

One range holds the tallest peak on Earth. Big rivers start in the snow up high on it.

Ranges form in a slow way. Big plates of rock push on each other. The land folds up over a long, long time.

Ranges change the weather, too. Wet wind drops rain on one slope. The other side can stay dry.

Ranges hold valleys, snow, and rock. Many plants and animals live on their slopes.

One big range is the Andes. It sits in South America, near the sea. Some of its peaks are old volcanoes. Llamas graze on its grassy slopes.

Another range is the Rocky Mountains. It sits in North America. Rivers start high on its slopes. Some flow west, and some flow east.

The Alps sit in Europe. People ski on the snowy slopes there each winter. The Alps form a border between a few countries.

The Himalayas sit in Asia. They hold the tallest peak on Earth. Big rivers start in the deep snow high on this range.

Ranges form in a very slow way. Huge plates of rock push against each other. The land folds upward over millions of years.

Ranges change the weather, too. Wet wind blows in and drops rain on one slope. The far side of the range can stay dry.

Ranges hold deep valleys, snow, and bare rock. Many kinds of plants and animals live on their slopes.

One huge range is the Andes. It runs down one side of South America, near the sea. Many of its peaks are old volcanoes. Llamas graze on its grassy slopes.

Another range is the Rocky Mountains, in North America. Rivers begin high on its slopes. Some flow west, and others flow east across the land.

The Alps rise up in Europe. Many people ski on the steep, snowy slopes each winter. The Alps even form a border between a few countries.

The Himalayas tower over Asia. They hold the tallest peak on Earth. Great rivers begin as melting snow high on this mighty range.

Mountain ranges form in a very slow way. Huge plates of rock deep in the ground push against each other. Over millions of years, the land folds upward into peaks.

Ranges also change the weather around them. Wet wind blows in from the sea and drops its rain on one slope. The far side of the range can stay dry for a long time.

Ranges hold deep valleys, snow, and bare rock. Each slope has its own small climate. Many plants and animals can live on a single range.

versions.title: Great Mountain Ranges
versions.text:
When people picture a mountain, they often think of just one peak. But mountains usually rise in long lines called ranges. Ranges rise up on every continent, and each one looks different.

One huge range is the Andes, in South America. It runs down the west side, near the sea. It is the longest range above the sea on Earth. Many of its peaks are old volcanoes, and llamas graze on its slopes.

Another range is the Rocky Mountains, across North America. Rivers begin high on its slopes. Some flow west toward one ocean. Others flow east toward another ocean.

The Alps rise up across Europe, crossing several countries. Many people ski on the steep, snowy slopes each winter. The sharp peaks also form a border between some countries.

The Himalayas tower over Asia. They hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest. Great rivers begin as melting snow high on this mighty range.

Mountain ranges form in a very slow way, over millions of years. Huge plates of rock deep under the ground push against each other. The squeezed land folds upward into peaks.

Ranges also change the weather around them. Wet wind blows in from the sea, rises up one slope, and drops its rain there. The far side can stay dry for a long time.

Ranges hold deep valleys, packed snow, and bare rock. Each slope has its own small climate. Many kinds of plants and animals can live on a single range.

versions.title: The Great Ranges of the World
versions.text:
When people picture a mountain, they often imagine just one tall peak. In fact, mountains usually rise in long lines called ranges. Ranges rise up on every continent, and each one looks and feels different from the rest.

One of the largest ranges is the Andes, in South America. It runs down the entire west side of the continent, near the sea. It is the longest range above sea level on the planet. Many of its peaks are old volcanoes, and llamas graze on its grassy slopes.

Another well-known range is the Rocky Mountains, across North America. Rivers begin high on its slopes. Some flow west toward the Pacific Ocean, while others flow east across wide plains.

The Alps rise up across Europe, crossing several countries. Millions of tourists ski on the steep, snowy slopes each winter. The sharp peaks also form a border between some of these countries.

The Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest. Great rivers that many people depend on begin as melting snow and glacier ice high on this mighty range.

Mountain ranges form in an extremely slow way, over millions of years. Huge plates of rock deep under the ground, called tectonic plates, push against each other. The squeezed land folds upward into tall peaks at a high elevation.

Ranges also change the climate around them. Wet wind blows in from the sea, rises up one slope, and drops its rain there. The far side of the range can stay very dry for a long time.

Ranges hold deep valleys carved by erosion, packed snow, bare rock, and valuable resources. Because each slope has its own small climate, a surprising number of plants and animals can live within a single range.

The Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest. Great rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on for water begin as melting snow and glacier ice high on this mighty range.

Mountain ranges generally form in an extremely slow way, over millions of years. Huge plates of rock deep under the ground, called tectonic plates, push against one another, and the squeezed land folds upward into tall peaks.

Ranges also change the climate around them in important ways. Wet wind blows in from the sea, rises up one slope, cools, and drops its rain there. The far side of the range, often called the dry side, can remain arid for a very long time.

Ranges hold deep valleys carved by erosion, packed snow, bare rock, and mineral resources buried below the surface. Because each slope has its own small climate, a surprising number of plants and animals can live within a single range, each suited to a particular elevation.

versions.title: The Great Ranges of the World
versions.text:
Studying a world map closely shows that mountains usually rise in long lines called ranges rather than standing alone. Ranges rise up on every continent on Earth, and each one looks and feels different from the others, shaped by its own history and location.

One of the largest ranges is the Andes, which extends down the entire western side of South America, close to the Pacific Ocean. This makes it the longest range above sea level on the planet. Many of its peaks are old volcanoes, and herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes. Farmers in the Andes were among the first in the world to grow potatoes, long ago.

Another well-known range is the Rocky Mountains, stretching across the western United States and into Canada. A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge and decides which way rivers flow. Rivers on the western side flow toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side flow toward the Atlantic.

The Alps rise up across Europe, crossing France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Millions of tourists ski on the steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks form a border between several of these countries.

The Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest. Great rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on for water begin as melting snow and glacier ice high on this mighty range, which formed when one huge plate of rock slowly crashed into another.

Mountain ranges generally form in this same slow way, over millions of years. Huge plates of rock deep under the ground, called tectonic plates, push against one another, and the squeezed land along their edges folds upward into tall peaks.

Ranges also change the climate around them in important ways. Wet wind blows in from the sea, rises up one slope, cools, and drops its rain there. The far side of the range, often called the dry side, can remain arid for a very long time.

Ranges hold deep valleys carved by erosion, packed snow, bare rock, and mineral resources buried below the surface. Because each slope has its own small climate, a surprising number of plants and animals can live within a single range, each suited to a particular elevation.

versions.title: How Mountain Ranges Shape the World
versions.text:
A look at a world map shows that mountains usually rise in long lines called ranges rather than standing alone, and these ranges rise up on every continent, each one shaped by its own distinctive history and location.

One of the largest is the Andes, which extends along the entire western edge of South America, close to the Pacific Ocean, making it the longest range above sea level on the planet. Many of its peaks are dormant volcanoes, and herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes. Farmers in the Andes were among the first in the world to cultivate potatoes, a crop that now feeds people on nearly every continent.

Another well-known range is the Rocky Mountains, stretching across the western United States and into Canada. A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge, deciding which way rivers flow; those on the western side head toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side cross the plains toward the Atlantic.

The Alps rise across Europe, crossing France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Millions of tourists ski on their steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks form a natural boundary between several of these countries, much as the Andes separate Chile from Argentina.

Far to the east, the Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest. Great rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on for water begin as melting snow and glacier ice high on this mighty range, which formed as one huge tectonic plate slowly collided with another over millions of years.

Mountain ranges generally form through this same slow collision of rock. Huge tectonic plates deep beneath the surface push against one another, and the compressed land along their edges folds upward into towering peaks. Along the western edge of South America, one plate is even sliding beneath another, a process called subduction, lifting the Andes a little higher almost every year.

Ranges reshape the climate around them in important ways. Moist wind blowing in from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and drops its rain there, so the far side of the range, often called the rain shadow, can stay arid for centuries, supporting only hardy desert plants.

Ranges also hold deep valleys carved by erosion, packed snow, bare rock, and mineral resources buried below the surface. Because each slope has its own small climate, a surprising diversity of plants and animals, or biodiversity, can live within a single range, each species isolated at a particular elevation.

versions.title: How Mountain Ranges Shape the World
versions.text:
A careful examination of a world map reveals long, winding lines of tall peaks rising above the surrounding terrain on every continent, each one shaped by its own distinctive geological history and location. A long chain of connected peaks is known as a mountain range, and no two ranges are entirely alike in their origin, shape, or character.

One of the largest is the Andes, which extends along the entire western edge of South America, close to the Pacific Ocean, making it the longest continuous range above sea level anywhere on the planet. Many of its peaks are dormant volcanoes, and herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes. Farmers in the Andes were among the first people in the world to cultivate potatoes, a crop that now feeds populations on nearly every continent on Earth, including many far beyond South America.

Another prominent range is the Rocky Mountains, stretching from Canada through the western United States. A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge, determining the ultimate direction in which rivers flow; those beginning on the western side flow toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side cross the wide plains toward the distant Atlantic Ocean.

The Alps rise across Europe, crossing France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Millions of tourists ski on their steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks even form a natural boundary between several of these nations, much as the Andes separate Chile from Argentina on an entirely different continent far away.

Far to the east, the Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest, rising more than eight thousand meters above sea level. Great rivers on which hundreds of millions of people depend for water begin as melting snow high on this mighty range, which formed as one enormous tectonic plate slowly collided with another over tens of millions of years, a process still measured by scientists today.

Mountain ranges generally form through this same slow collision of rock. Huge tectonic plates deep beneath the surface push against one another, and the compressed land along their edges folds upward into towering peaks. Along the western edge of South America, one plate is even sliding beneath another in a process known as subduction, lifting the Andes a little higher nearly every year and occasionally triggering destructive earthquakes along the coast.

Ranges reshape the regional climate in significant and lasting ways. Moist wind blowing in from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and releases its rain there, so the far side of the range, often called the rain shadow, can remain arid for centuries, supporting only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce and unpredictable water.

Ranges also hold deep valleys, packed snow, bare rock, and valuable mineral resources buried far below the surface. Because each slope and valley forms its own small climate, a surprising diversity of plants and animals can live within a single range, each species isolated at a particular elevation and adapted to conditions found nowhere else nearby, a pattern that continues to fascinate biologists who study biodiversity across the world's great ranges.

Many of its peaks are dormant volcanoes, and herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes. Farmers in the Andes were among the first people in the world to cultivate potatoes, a crop that now feeds populations on nearly every continent on Earth, including many regions far beyond South America that once had no idea the plant existed.

A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge, determining the ultimate direction in which rivers flow; those beginning on the western side flow toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side cross the wide plains toward the distant Atlantic Ocean, sometimes traveling thousands of kilometers before reaching it.

Millions of tourists ski on their steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks even form a natural boundary between several of these nations, much as the Andes separate Chile from Argentina on an entirely different continent far away, demonstrating how mountains repeatedly define political borders worldwide.

Great rivers on which hundreds of millions of people depend for water begin as melting snow high on this mighty range, which formed as one enormous tectonic plate slowly collided with another over tens of millions of years, a process still measured carefully by scientists today using satellites.

Mountain ranges generally form through this same slow collision of rock. Huge tectonic plates deep beneath the surface push against one another, and the compressed land along their edges folds upward into towering peaks. Along the western edge of South America, one plate is even sliding beneath another in a process known as subduction, lifting the Andes a little higher nearly every year and occasionally triggering destructive earthquakes along the crowded coast.

Moist wind blowing in from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and releases its rain there, so the far side of the range, often called the rain shadow, can remain arid for centuries, supporting only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce and unpredictable water, like those found east of the Andes.

Because each slope and valley forms its own small climate, a surprising diversity of plants and animals can live within a single range, each species isolated at a particular elevation and adapted to conditions found nowhere else nearby, a pattern that continues to fascinate biologists who study biodiversity across the world's great ranges and the many creatures confined to them.

versions.title: How Mountain Ranges Shape the World
versions.text:
A careful examination of a world map reveals long, winding lines of tall peaks rising above the surrounding terrain on every continent, with each range shaped by its own distinctive geological history, climate, and location, despite the broadly similar forces that ultimately create them all. A long chain of connected peaks is known as a mountain range, and strikingly, no two ranges on Earth turn out to be entirely alike in their origin, shape, or character.

One of the largest is the Andes, which extends along the entire western edge of South America, close to the Pacific Ocean, making it the longest continuous range above sea level anywhere on the planet. Many of its peaks are dormant volcanoes, while herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes below. Farmers in the Andes were among the first people in the world to cultivate potatoes, a crop that now feeds populations on nearly every continent, including many regions that, centuries ago, had no idea the plant even existed.

Another prominent range, the Rocky Mountains, stretches from Canada through the western United States. A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge, determining the ultimate direction in which rivers flow across an entire continent; those beginning on the western side flow toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side cross the wide plains toward the distant Atlantic, sometimes traveling thousands of kilometers before finally reaching it.

The Alps, by contrast, rise across Europe, crossing France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Millions of tourists ski on their steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks even form a natural boundary between several of these nations, much as the Andes separate Chile from Argentina on an entirely different continent, illustrating how mountains repeatedly come to define political borders across the world.

Far to the east, the Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest, rising more than eight thousand meters above sea level. Great rivers on which hundreds of millions of people depend for water begin as melting snow high on this mighty range, which formed as one enormous tectonic plate slowly collided with another over tens of millions of years, a collision still measured precisely by scientists today using orbiting satellites.

Most mountain ranges, in fact, form through this same slow collision of rock, as huge tectonic plates deep beneath the surface push relentlessly against one another, folding the compressed land along their edges upward into towering peaks. Along the western edge of South America, one plate is even sliding beneath another in a process called subduction, lifting the Andes a little higher nearly every year while occasionally triggering destructive earthquakes along the densely populated coast.

Beyond simply existing, ranges actively reshape the regional climate around them. Moist wind blowing in from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and releases its rain there, so the far side of the range, known as the rain shadow, can remain arid for centuries, supporting only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce and unpredictable rainfall, much like those found east of the Andes.

Ranges also hold deep valleys, packed snow, bare rock, and valuable mineral resources buried far below the surface, resources that have drawn settlers and industries for generations. Because each slope and valley forms its own small climate, a surprising diversity of plants and animals can live within a single range, with each species isolated at a particular elevation and adapted to conditions found nowhere else nearby, a pattern that continues to fascinate biologists who study biodiversity across the world's great ranges.

versions.text:
A careful examination of a world map reveals long, winding lines of tall peaks rising above the surrounding terrain on every continent, with each range shaped by its own distinctive geological history, climate, and location, despite the broadly similar underlying forces that ultimately create them all. One of the largest is the Andes, which extends along the entire western edge of South America, close to the Pacific Ocean, making it the longest continuous range above sea level anywhere on the planet. Many of its peaks are dormant volcanoes, while herds of llamas and alpacas graze on its grassy slopes below, largely undisturbed. Farmers in the Andes were among the first people in the world to cultivate potatoes, a crop that now feeds enormous populations on nearly every continent, including many regions that, centuries ago, had no idea the plant even existed until explorers carried it across the ocean.

Another prominent range, the Rocky Mountains, stretches from Canada through the western United States. A line called the Continental Divide runs along its highest ridge, determining the ultimate direction in which rivers flow across an entire continent; those beginning on the western side flow toward the Pacific, while those on the eastern side cross the wide plains toward the distant Atlantic, sometimes traveling thousands of kilometers before finally reaching it.

The Alps, by striking contrast, rise across Europe, crossing France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria. Millions of tourists ski on their steep, snowy slopes each winter, and the sharp peaks even form a natural boundary between several of these nations, much as the Andes separate Chile from Argentina on an entirely different continent, illustrating how mountains have repeatedly come to define political borders across the world throughout history.

Far to the east, the Himalayas tower over Asia and hold the tallest peak on Earth, Mount Everest, rising more than eight thousand meters above sea level. Great rivers on which hundreds of millions of people depend for water begin as melting snow high on this mighty range, which formed as one enormous tectonic plate slowly collided with another over tens of millions of years, a collision still measured with remarkable precision by scientists today using orbiting satellites.

Most mountain ranges, in fact, form through this same slow collision of rock, as huge tectonic plates deep beneath the surface push relentlessly against one another, folding the compressed land along their edges upward into towering peaks over immense stretches of time. Along the western edge of South America, one plate is even sliding beneath another in a process called subduction, lifting the Andes a little higher nearly every year while occasionally triggering destructive earthquakes along the densely populated coast below.

Beyond simply existing as scenery, ranges actively reshape the regional climate around them. Moist wind blowing in from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and releases its rain there, so the far side of the range, known as the rain shadow, can remain arid for centuries at a stretch, supporting only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce and unpredictable rainfall, much like those found east of the Andes in Patagonia.

Ranges also hold deep valleys, packed snow, bare rock, and valuable mineral resources buried far below the surface, resources that have drawn settlers, miners, and entire industries for generations. Because each slope and valley forms its own small climate, a surprising diversity of plants and animals can live within a single range, with each species isolated at a particular elevation and adapted to conditions found nowhere else nearby, a pattern that continues to fascinate biologists who study biodiversity across the world's great ranges and the many creatures confined within them.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: A tour of famous mountain ranges and how they shape the world
How to grow potatoes on a small farm in the north
A trip to ski in the country of Austria with some friends and family
Why llamas live only in zoos around the world today
questions.why: The article describes several mountain ranges, where they are, and how they affect weather, borders, and wildlife.

wrong.B: Potatoes are only one small detail about the Andes.
wrong.C: Skiing in the Alps is one detail, not the whole article.
wrong.D: The article mentions llamas living on mountain slopes, not in zoos.

On the west side of South America

On a small island in the Pacific

It is a type of weather in the mountains.
It is a border between two oceans.
questions.why: The sentence explains that rivers starting on one side of the Divide flow one way, and rivers on the other side flow the other way.

wrong.A: A divide is a line on a mountain, not a city.
wrong.C: A divide is about where rivers flow, not weather.
wrong.D: The Divide is a line in the mountains, not an ocean border.

questions.stem: Why did the author write this article?
options: To tell a made-up story about a brave mountain climber
To teach readers about several real mountain ranges
To list every single peak on Earth by height
To convince readers to move to the mountains
questions.why: The article gives true facts about the Andes, Rockies, Alps, and Himalayas and how ranges form and shape the land.

wrong.A: The article is nonfiction, with real facts, not a made-up story.
wrong.C: The article names only a few ranges and peaks, not every one on Earth.
wrong.D: The article is informative, not trying to convince anyone to move.

questions.stem: What happens when big plates of rock push together?
options: The land folds upward into tall peaks over time.
The land turns into flat, dry desert instantly.
The ocean dries up completely.
All the rivers stop flowing at once.

wrong.B: The article does not say the land turns to desert right away.
wrong.C: The article does not mention oceans drying up.
wrong.D: The article does not say rivers stop; it says rivers begin on mountain slopes.

LOW.prompt: Pick one mountain range from the article. Tell two facts about it and explain why you find it interesting.
checklist: I named one mountain range from the article.
I used at least two facts from the article.

LOW.modelAnswer: I find the Andes very interesting because it is the longest mountain range above sea level on Earth. I also learned that farmers there first grew potatoes long ago. I would like to see llamas grazing on its grassy slopes someday.

keyWords.definition: the height of a place above sea level
keyWords.example: The small town sits at a high elevation in the hills.

keyWords.definition: something useful that people can take from nature and use

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Skiing is the most popular sport in the Alps every winter, and it is the reason people visit mountains.
Mountain ranges around the world differ in location but all shape climate, borders, and life nearby.
The Rocky Mountains are taller than the Himalayas, and they are the highest range in the world.
Llamas can only survive on the slopes of the Andes, and no other mountain range has animals.
questions.why: The article compares several ranges and explains how each one, in its own way, affects weather, borders, and the plants and animals around it.

wrong.A: Skiing is one detail about the Alps, not the main idea.
wrong.C: The article never compares the height of the Rockies to the Himalayas; Everest is described as the tallest peak on Earth.
wrong.D: The article only says llamas live on the Andes, not that they can live nowhere else.

questions.stem: According to the article, what splits the direction rivers flow in the Rocky Mountains?
options: The Pacific Ocean
The Continental Divide
A line of old volcanoes
A border between countries

wrong.A: The Pacific Ocean is where some rivers end up, not the line that splits them.
wrong.C: Volcanoes are mentioned for the Andes, not for splitting rivers in the Rockies.
wrong.D: A border is a different idea from the Continental Divide.

questions.stem: What crop did farmers in the Andes first grow, according to the article?
options: Wheat
Rice
Potatoes
Corn

wrong.B: Rice is not mentioned at all.
wrong.D: Corn is not named in the article.

questions.stem: Why might a dry desert form on one side of a mountain range?
options: The wet wind drops most of its rain on the near slope first.
People built dams that stop all the rainwater from reaching the far side.
The far side of the range gets no sunlight at all during the year.
Mountains always stop wind from moving at all across the land.
questions.why: The article explains that wind drops its rain on one slope while rising, leaving the far side, the rain shadow, dry.

wrong.B: The article does not mention dams.
wrong.C: The article does not say the far side gets no sunlight.
wrong.D: Wind still moves over and around mountains; it just loses its moisture.

questions.stem: The Andes form a border between Chile and Argentina, and the Alps form borders between several European countries. What does this suggest about mountain ranges?
options: They often naturally separate neighboring countries.
They always belong to only one country and cannot be shared.
They are too small to matter to any border or map.
They are found only in South America and Europe.
questions.why: Since both examples show ranges acting as natural boundaries between countries, this is a pattern across different continents.

wrong.B: Both examples describe ranges shared between more than one country.
wrong.C: The article describes these ranges as huge, not small.
wrong.D: The Alps example shows ranges acting this way in Europe too.

questions.stem: "The far side of the range, often called the dry side, can remain arid for a very long time." What does arid mean here?
options: Extremely dry
Very cold
Covered in snow
Full of rivers
questions.why: The sentence calls it the dry side right before using the word arid, showing that arid means extremely dry.

wrong.B: The sentence is about dryness, not temperature.
wrong.C: Arid land is dry, not snowy.
wrong.D: An arid area has little water, so it would not be full of rivers.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the middle of the article?
options: By describing one mountain range after another, one at a time
By listing every country in the world in alphabetical order
By telling a single story about one family's mountain trip
By comparing only the prices of ski tickets in each country
questions.why: The article moves through the Andes, the Rocky Mountains, the Alps, and the Himalayas, describing each range in its own paragraph.

wrong.B: The article names only a few countries, not a full alphabetical list.
wrong.C: There is no single family's story in the article.
wrong.D: Ski ticket prices are never mentioned.

questions.stem: What happens along the western edge of South America, according to the article?
options: One plate slides beneath another, lifting the Andes higher.
The Andes shrink a little shorter every single year.
Rivers stop flowing because of the dry climate.
Volcanoes there have all become extinct forever.
questions.why: The article explains that along this coast, one plate slides beneath another, slowly lifting the Andes higher and sometimes causing earthquakes.

wrong.B: The article says the Andes get higher, not shorter.
wrong.C: Rivers are described as beginning in the mountains, not stopping.
wrong.D: The article calls some Andes peaks old volcanoes, but does not say every one is extinct.

MID.prompt: Explain how a mountain range can affect both the weather and the borders of a region. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained an effect on weather.
I explained an effect on borders.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: A mountain range affects weather because wet wind from the sea rises up one slope, cools, and drops rain there, leaving the far side dry for a long time. A mountain range can also affect borders, since the Alps separate parts of France, Switzerland, Italy, and Austria, just like the Andes separate Chile from Argentina. These examples show how the same range can shape both climate and country lines.

keyWords.definition: relating to the huge moving plates of rock that make up Earth's outer layer
keyWords.example: Scientists study tectonic activity to understand earthquakes.

keyWords.definition: the process in which one tectonic plate slides down beneath another
keyWords.example: Subduction along the coast can cause powerful earthquakes.

keyWords.definition: the wide variety of different living things found in a place
keyWords.example: A rainforest has far more biodiversity than a parking lot.

keyWords.definition: extremely dry, with very little rainfall
keyWords.example: Few crops can grow in such an arid climate.

keyWords.definition: separated from others and existing alone
keyWords.example: The isolated village had no road connecting it to the city.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Every mountain range on Earth formed in exactly the same way, from the same kind of pushing plates.
Mountain ranges differ in origin and location but consistently shape regional climate, borders, and biodiversity.
The Himalayas are more important than any other range on Earth, and the others do not matter at all to people or to science.
Subduction only happens along the coast of South America, and nowhere else on the planet at all.
questions.why: The article shows several ranges with different origins and locations, then explains the shared ways ranges influence climate, political borders, and biodiversity.

wrong.A: The article actually shows that ranges form in somewhat different ways and settings.
wrong.C: The article treats each range as significant in its own way, not one as most important.
wrong.D: Subduction is given as one example near South America, not a rule limited to that coast.

questions.stem: According to the article, what forms when a tectonic plate slides beneath another one?
options: A process called subduction, which can lift mountains higher.
A new ocean that quickly fills with water and then dries up again.
A desert that forms only in Europe, near the old cities.
A permanent border between two oceans, which can never move.
questions.why: The article describes subduction along South America's coast as the plate sliding beneath another, lifting the Andes and sometimes causing earthquakes.

wrong.B: The article does not describe a new ocean forming.
wrong.C: Subduction is linked to South America in the article, not Europe's deserts.
wrong.D: Subduction is about plates and mountains, not ocean borders.

questions.stem: What does the article say about the rain shadow on the dry side of a range?
options: It is always covered in thick, green forests and rivers.
It receives more rain than the wet side of the range does.
It supports only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce water.
It disappears completely after a few decades of dry weather.
questions.why: The article states that the arid far side of a range can remain dry for centuries, supporting only hardy desert plants adapted to scarce water.

wrong.A: Thick forests are more likely on the wet, rainy slope, not the rain shadow.
wrong.B: The rain shadow receives less rain, since the wet slope captures the moisture first.
wrong.D: The article suggests this dryness can last for centuries, not disappear quickly.

questions.stem: Why might scientists expect many unique species to evolve across a single mountain range?
options: Every elevation on a range has identical weather and soil, so every place has the same species.
Mountains prevent any living thing from surviving above the level of the sea, so no species lives there.
All mountain animals migrate to the same single valley each year, so they all mix together and stay alike.
Different elevations create separate small climates that can isolate species from one another.
questions.why: Because each slope and valley has its own small climate, species can become isolated at particular elevations and adapt differently, increasing biodiversity.

wrong.A: The article specifically says each slope and valley has its own small climate, not identical conditions.
wrong.B: The article describes llamas, alpacas, and other wildlife thriving on mountain slopes.
wrong.C: The article does not describe animals migrating to one shared valley.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why the Andes continue to rise in elevation almost every year?
options: Ongoing subduction along the coast keeps pushing and lifting the rock upward.
Farmers add new soil to the mountainside each planting season to make it taller.
Melting glaciers make the mountain rock expand and swell like a sponge each year.
Tourists visiting the slopes gradually pack the rock down tighter every summer.
questions.why: The article links the Andes' continued rise directly to the ongoing subduction process along South America's western coast.

wrong.B: The article does not mention farmers adding soil to raise elevation.
wrong.C: The article does not claim melting ice expands the rock itself.
wrong.D: Tourism is mentioned for the Alps, not as a cause of the Andes rising.

questions.stem: "A surprising diversity of plants and animals can live within a single range... a pattern that continues to fascinate biologists who study biodiversity." What does biodiversity mean here?
options: The height of a mountain above sea level
The wide variety of different living things in an area
The process of one plate sliding beneath another
The dry conditions found on one side of a range
questions.why: The sentence connects biodiversity directly to the surprising variety of plants and animals found across a range's different elevations.

wrong.A: Height above sea level is elevation, a separate idea in the article.
wrong.C: That process is subduction, discussed earlier in the article.
wrong.D: Dry conditions describe the rain shadow, not biodiversity.

questions.stem: Why does the author move from describing individual ranges to explaining how ranges form and reshape climate and life?
options: To prove that the Andes are the only range worth studying closely at school.
To argue that mountain tourism should be banned worldwide for many years.
To contradict the earlier descriptions of each named range in the article.
To shift from specific examples toward the shared forces and effects behind them.
questions.why: After introducing several distinct ranges, the article turns to the common tectonic processes and effects, such as rain shadows and biodiversity, that connect them.

wrong.A: The Andes receive extended description, but the Alps and Himalayas remain important examples too.
wrong.B: The article mentions tourism neutrally, without arguing against it.
wrong.C: The later explanation supports the earlier descriptions rather than contradicting them.

questions.stem: How do the Andes and the Alps compare as examples of mountain ranges forming borders?
options: Only the Andes form a border; the Alps do not touch any country lines or neighbors.
Both ranges separate neighboring countries, despite sitting on different continents.
Only the Alps involve any volcanic activity at all, while the Andes have none.
Neither range is ever associated with any national border between two lands.
questions.why: The article explicitly compares the Andes, which separate Chile and Argentina, with the Alps, which form boundaries among several European nations.

wrong.A: The article describes the Alps as forming boundaries too.
wrong.C: Volcanic activity is mentioned for the Andes, not specifically for the Alps.
wrong.D: Both ranges are directly tied to national borders in the article.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how tectonic forces both build mountain ranges and shape the climate and biodiversity around them. Use specific evidence from the article to connect cause and effect.
checklist: I explained how tectonic plates build mountain ranges.
I connected elevation or climate to biodiversity.
I used specific evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Tectonic plates slowly collide or slide beneath one another in a process called subduction, folding and lifting rock into towering ranges like the Andes and the Himalayas over millions of years. Once a range exists, it reshapes the climate around it: moist wind drops its rain on one slope, leaving the far side arid for centuries, as seen in the rain shadow east of the Andes. Because elevation also creates many small, separate climates on a single range, species can become isolated at particular heights and evolve differently, which is why mountain ranges support such striking biodiversity across relatively short distances.
